text: Scope tells you which systems are in bounds. This lesson covers a completely different question: how much does the tester already know about those systems before testing even starts. Source code, architecture diagrams, credentials — withholding or providing that information is its own scoping decision, because it fundamentally changes what the engagement actually measures.

In a white-box engagement, the tester starts with everything — source code, architecture, credentials at multiple privilege levels — making it the fastest way to achieve thorough coverage, but the least realistic model of an actual attacker. Black-box gives the tester nothing beyond maybe a company name, the same starting position as a real external attacker, which makes it the most realistic simulation — but reconnaissance alone can eat the engagement clock before full coverage is reached. Gray-box sits in between, starting with partial knowledge like standard user credentials.

That partial-knowledge middle ground is exactly why gray-box is the most common choice for real-world engagements. It mirrors a genuinely common threat — an insider, or an attacker who already has a compromised low-privilege account. Because the tester isn't burning hours on reconnaissance a real attacker in that position wouldn't need either, gray-box covers meaningfully more ground than black-box within the same fixed time budget, while staying far more realistic than white-box.

Whichever model fits gets written into the scope and ROE before testing starts, the same way testing windows and in-scope systems are. A client asking 'could a random attacker with nothing get in' needs to specifically request black-box and budget for the time it takes. A client worried about a specific insider scenario should request gray-box with credentials that actually match it.

That closes out Chapter 1: real written authorization, a precise agreed-upon scope, a published methodology in PTES and the OWASP Testing Guide, and a deliberate choice of how much the tester knows going in. Every technique in the chapters ahead assumes all four of those are already settled, in writing, before anything else begins.
